most studied ecosystems in the world, which is Yellowstone National Park.
And Beatty was a scientist, a lawyer, a public servant, and when she assumed
leadership, she inherited a system that was already deep in conflict.
Ranchers, scientists, policymakers, federal agencies, local communities, and
landscapes were all entangled in competing priorities, and she stood at that
decision point with her team, and that decision was wolves.
So by the early 20th century, wolves had been systematically eradicated from
Yellowstone, and the last resident packs disappeared in the 1920s through hunting
and predator control programs, reflecting an assumption at the time that large
predators were inherently harmful.
So what followed ended up not being a system that was frozen in the wolves'
absence, but one where elk, bison, vegetation, other predators, climate, fire,
hydrology, human management, and more continued interacting.
Removing the wolf had not removed complexity.
It had just removed one set of relationships from an already complex system.
And restoring these relationships meant returning an apex predator to a landscape
from which it had been absent for roughly 70 years while under extreme scrutiny and
opposition. Understandably so, ranchers feared for their livestock.
Communities questioned the necessity.
Scientists could anticipate some outcomes, but they could not specify precisely how
an ecosystem this complex would respond.
But nevertheless, in January 1995, 14 wolves from Canada entered
Yellowstone, with 17 following the next year, and that was 14 animals initially
against 2.2 million acres with no precise model of what was to follow.
And what ended up following became one of the most iconic and maybe most debated
examples of a trophic cascade, which is the process where changes at one trophic
level can propagate indirectly through others.
But trophic cascades are not simple chains of cause and effect.
They unfold within networks. Their effects can be nonlinear, spatially uneven,
delayed, amplified, weakened, and redirected by processes
occurring elsewhere in the system.
So wolves did not simply return and reduce elk populations.
Their return altered predation pressure within a system that also contained other

Browsing pressure also changed. And aspen and willow recovered in some places while
not in others. And beaver populations increased, and bison expanded.
And to this day, scientists continue debating the relative importance of these
pathways. And what emerged was not the simple chain of wolves changed elk,
elk released vegetation, vegetation restored the rivers.
There was something infinitely more interesting happening, and that is a network of

So no individual wolf contained a blueprint for Yellowstone.
They didn't know how to restore an aspen stand, and no elk knew that it was

System-level change emerged from interactions among these components because

Change one relationship, and other relationships respond. The system reorganizes.

wolves mattered not simply because wolves were present, but because their presence

Similarly, data does not become valuable simply because it exists in a repository

A new dataset enters an infrastructure. That arrival becomes an event.
A workflow is triggered. A product is updated.
A model can be recalibrated, and now an analysis has become possible.
And other datasets can now acquire new context, and those outputs themselves can

And this perspective is what motivates the architectural approach taken in my
research, which is event-driven modular systems informed by microservices
architecture paradigms. In these systems, components are designed to be loosely
coupled but highly responsive. And rather than enforcing one monolithic pipeline in
which every component must change together, microservices allow functions such as
data ingestion, processing, analysis, transformation, and dissemination to operate
independently while communicating through well-defined interfaces, protocols, and
responding dynamically to events in the larger system.
So no individual service contains a blueprint for the entire information ecosystem.
System-level behavior emerges through coordination among them.
So this architecture is scalable not only computationally but sociotechnically.
So new components can be introduced without requiring the entire system to be
redesigned, and different organizations can maintain their own services while
participating in a shared information ecosystem through standards, interfaces, and
event exchanges.
In this way, microservices enable a form of coordination without requiring the
burden of complete centralization.
But loosely coupled, by no means, is structureless.
There remains a necessary layer of shared structure, typically through standards

respond to one another. So this shared structure does not eliminate difference.
It creates conditions under which difference can coexist productively.
So this is also not entirely foreign to biodiversity informatics.
